title: Who Is a Candidate for Dental Implants? A Complete Guide

body:
If you are wondering whether you are a candidate for dental implants, you are in good company. Many patients visit our [dental implants](/services/dental-implants/) page after hearing implants recommended, and they want a clear, realistic checklist before booking imaging and a consultation. This guide from Dr. Nuriel Lavi at Valencia Dentistry in Santa Clarita walks through the clinical criteria, the health and lifestyle factors that matter, the concerns patients raise most often and the questions to bring to your consult.

## How clinicians decide: the five pillars

Candidacy is assessed by combining an oral exam, a cone beam CT (CBCT) scan, your medical history and your expectations. In practice the decision comes down to five pillars:

- **Bone and anatomy:** enough jawbone where the implant will sit, or willingness to accept grafting or an alternative anchoring technique.
- **Gum and periodontal health:** controlled gum disease, or a clear plan to treat it before implant placement.
- **Medical stability:** controlled metabolic disease such as diabetes, cardiac clearance when needed, and careful review of medications such as bisphosphonates.
- **Lifestyle factors:** smoking and vaping raise failure risk; willingness to stop during healing improves outcomes.
- **Realistic expectations and maintenance:** readiness for lifelong hygiene and periodic professional checks to prevent peri-implant disease.

## Medical conditions that affect candidacy

Not every health issue rules you out, but some change timing, technique or risk.

- **Diabetes.** Well-controlled diabetes is usually compatible with implants; poorly controlled blood glucose raises the risk of infection and slow healing. Guidelines treat control as the deciding factor; see the systematic review at the [National Library of Medicine](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4647895/).
- **Osteoporosis and bone medications.** Oral bisphosphonates need careful discussion; intravenous bisphosphonates for metastatic disease carry higher risk and often need clearance from several specialists.
- **Smoking and vaping.** Smoking consistently shows higher complication rates. Most clinicians advise stopping before surgery and throughout osseointegration, the period when bone bonds to the implant.
- **Autoimmune conditions and radiation.** Recent head or neck radiation and active immunosuppression change candidacy and usually call for specialist input.

## Oral health matters more than age

Chronological age is rarely the main issue. Implants are placed successfully in patients from their 20s to their 80s when medical and oral health are optimized. Focus instead on bone volume, gum disease control and whether you can commit to aftercare. For older adults, see our notes on [dental implants for seniors](/dental-implants-for-seniors-safety-success/).

## Common scenarios and practical options

Here are the pathways typically proposed depending on what the CBCT and exam show.

- **Sufficient bone, healthy gums:** a straightforward implant and crown, or an implant-retained prosthesis.
- **Bone deficiency at a single site:** localized grafting or ridge augmentation followed by implant placement, or a narrower implant in select locations.
- **Extensive bone loss in an arch:** staged grafting, zygomatic implants for severe upper-jaw resorption, or full-arch options described in our [All-on-X guide](/what-is-all-on-x-complete-guide/).
- **Active periodontal disease:** treat the gum disease first, then re-evaluate once inflammation is controlled.

| Factor | Ideal candidate | When implants are still possible |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bone volume | Bone height and width present for a standard implant (confirmed on CBCT) | Short implants, grafting or alternative anchorage such as zygomatic implants |
| Periodontal health | Healthy gums and stable probing depths | After periodontal therapy and a maintenance program |
| Diabetes | HbA1c in target range and stable | With tighter monitoring and medical co-management |
| Smoking | Non-smoker, or willing to stop around surgery | Cessation improves candidacy; risk stays higher if smoking continues |

## What the evidence says about success and risk

Systematic reviews commonly report long-term implant survival between 90 and 98 percent over 10 years, but those figures depend on patient factors and prosthesis type; the review at the [National Library of Medicine](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4647895/) is a good starting point. Survival of the fixture is one measure; prosthetic complications, maintenance needs and peri-implant disease are separate concerns covered during consent.

## What patients worry about most

The concerns people raise most often before booking imaging shape how we talk to patients:

- **Hidden costs.** Patients frequently receive a quote and then see extra line items for grafts, lab work or provisional teeth. Ask for an itemized estimate that lists surgery, implants, abutments, temporary teeth, lab fees and follow-ups.
- **Medical risks misunderstood.** Being told you are not a candidate because of bone loss, or that grafting will add months to the plan, is a common and medically reasonable caution rather than a brush-off.
- **Access and timing.** Specialist or teaching-clinic backlogs can lengthen timelines. If timing and budget matter, factor scheduling into your decision.

## Cost reality: typical ranges and a lifetime view

Prices vary by implant system, prosthesis type and whether grafting is needed. Our [Dental Implants Valencia Cost Guide](/dental-implants-valencia-cost-guide/) gives a local breakdown for single-tooth and full-arch options. The ranges below are typical U.S. figures, not Valencia Dentistry fees.

| Treatment | Typical upfront cost (U.S.) | Lifetime notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-tooth implant and crown | $3,000 to $6,000 per tooth | Higher initial cost; preserves bone; crown may need replacement in 10 to 15 years |
| Implant-retained overdenture | $7,000 to $25,000 per arch | Lower cost than a fixed arch; better stability than a conventional denture |
| Full-arch fixed (All-on-X) | $15,000 to $50,000 per arch | Fewer implants per arch; immediate provisional often possible; prosthesis renewal over the years |
| Conventional denture | $600 to $8,000 for both arches | Lowest upfront cost; ongoing relines and progressive ridge resorption |

## Questions to bring to your consult

- Bring or request a CBCT scan. It is the single most useful test for bone and anatomy.
- Ask for a written, itemized estimate: surgeon fee, implant fixtures, abutments, provisional prosthesis, lab costs, grafting and follow-up visits.
- Which implant system is used, and why? Are the parts proprietary?
- How are medical risks such as diabetes, anticoagulant therapy or bisphosphonate exposure managed?
- What happens if an implant fails to integrate?
- Request before-and-after cases with anatomy and age similar to yours.

## How to improve your chances

Small steps before surgery improve outcomes and widen your options:

- Stop smoking at least several weeks before surgery and through osseointegration if possible.
- Control conditions such as diabetes and share recent lab values.
- Treat gum disease first; healthy periodontal tissue lowers the risk of peri-implantitis.
- Keep up excellent oral hygiene and plan for lifelong maintenance visits.

## Next steps

Whether you are a candidate for dental implants comes down to an individual assessment of bone, gum health, medical stability, lifestyle and expectations. Dr. Lavi uses 3D CBCT imaging and guided implant planning to give you a clear, written plan, and you see his at every visit. For related reading, see [how long dental implants take](/how-long-do-dental-implants-take/) and our [bone grafting for dental implants](/bone-grafting-for-dental-implants-guide/) guide, then schedule an imaging appointment through our [dental implants](/services/dental-implants/) page or call (661) 254-5200.

faq.q: Am I a candidate for dental implants if I have diabetes?
faq.a: Many people with diabetes are candidates when blood glucose is well controlled. Poor control raises infection and healing risks, so bring recent lab results and expect coordination with your physician. Elective implant surgery is often delayed until control improves.

faq.q: Can I smoke after implant surgery?
faq.a: Smoking raises the risk of implant failure and peri-implantitis. Most clinicians recommend stopping before surgery and throughout healing. Even long-term smokers who quit around the procedure tend to do better than those who continue.

faq.q: I was told I lack bone. Does that rule out implants?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Options include localized bone grafting, a sinus lift for the upper jaw, short or narrow implants, zygomatic implants for severe upper-jaw bone loss, or an implant-retained overdenture. Each has different cost and timeline implications.

faq.q: How much will it cost, and will insurance pay?
faq.a: Cost depends on the number of implants, whether grafting is needed and the prosthetic design. Some insurers cover parts such as diagnostics or crowns but often treat implants as elective. Get pre-authorization and an itemized estimate, and see our Dental Implants Valencia Cost Guide.

faq.q: Am I too old for implants?
faq.a: Age alone is rarely a reason to decline implants. Candidates range from young adults to seniors. What matters is overall health, bone quality and the ability to maintain oral hygiene over the long term.

faq.q: How long is recovery, and does it hurt?
faq.a: Post-operative discomfort is usually managed with standard medication. Initial healing takes days to weeks; osseointegration commonly takes three to six months. In select cases a provisional tooth can be placed the same day, but the bone still needs time to integrate.
